# Typed harness configuration

`workingDirectory` selects an existing workspace-relative directory for all four
harnesses, including both Codex transports. `agent.exec()` and agent turns run
there; `agent.workspace` and scorer paths still refer to the copied root.
Absolute paths, parent traversal, and escaping symlinks are rejected. Each trial
gets its own workspace and HOME, but cwd is not an operating-system sandbox.
For enforced filesystem isolation, combine the profile with the existing
`isolation: { mode: 'strict', readOnlyPaths }` contract. App-only staging needs
no `workingDirectory`: the copied app is already the execution root.

OpenCode profiles are typed against the pinned runtime. The same exports are
available through `@wix/agent-evals`.

```typescript
import { createAgent, type OpenCodeOptions } from '@wix/pathgrade';

const profile = {
    defaultAgent: 'author',
    agents: {
        author: { mode: 'primary', tools: { read: false, 'batch-read': true } },
        reviewer: { mode: 'subagent', prompt: 'Review existing code.' },
    },
    managedTools: { 'batch-read': '/trusted/batch-read.ts' },
    toolActions: { 'batch-read': 'read_file' },
    config: { lsp: false, compaction: { prune: true } },
    runtime: { prune: true },
} satisfies OpenCodeOptions;

const agent = await createAgent({
    agent: 'opencode',
    opencodeExecutable: '/trusted/opencode-v1.18.14',
    workspace: './fixture',
    workingDirectory: 'app',
    model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6',
    opencode: profile,
});
try {
    await agent.prompt('Implement the requested component.');
} finally {
    await agent.dispose();
}
```

`managedPlugins` and `managedTools` stage explicit trusted `.ts`, `.js`, or `.mjs`
regular files into private HOME before boundary creation. The pinned loader only
discovers `.js`/`.ts`, so `.mjs` inputs are staged as `.js` with unchanged contents.
Source symlinks are rejected. PathGrade stages a private compatibility package
for the SDK root and `/tool` entry points: the identity `tool()` builder and `tool.schema` backed by PathGrade’s
Zod dependency. It has no host dependency links or registry install during staging.
Bundle other imports/dependencies, including advanced SDK entry points.
Skill/instruction paths must remain inside the selected cwd. Permission overrides must preserve
deny-by-default external-directory access; narrow trusted dependency exceptions
are allowed. Sharing, auto-updates, MCP mounting, and managed environment paths
remain owned by PathGrade. Provider tuning allows cache/timeout options and model
filters; credentials and endpoints must use validated environment variables.
Additional runtime-recognized model names require an API-key-only
`opencode.modelContract`. Native tool availability and agent definitions are
OpenCode-only fields; Codex's `transport` is Codex-only. Invalid cross-harness
combinations fail in the editor and at runtime. The fixed Scenario V2 ACP runtime
does not accept `opencode` customization.

For a default-deny primary agent with a reviewer, also set
`agents.author.permission.task` to `{ '*': 'deny', reviewer: 'allow' }`.

For optional real-runtime verification, set `PATHGRADE_OPENCODE_EXECUTABLE` to
the pinned binary and run `yarn test` in the PathGrade package. The contract test
uses a loopback model server and proves plugin-hook execution, custom-tool
execution, tool-list overrides, reviewer invocation, trace mapping, and resume.

## Generic profiles and deterministic configuration

PathGrade contains no application-specific agents, prompts, tools, delegation
rules, or result parsers. Consumer profiles own those definitions. Profile options
are snapshotted at creation; runtime/dependency versions must remain pinned.

Agent selection uses `opencode.defaultAgent`, then native `config.default_agent`,
then `build`. Main-model selection uses `AgentOptions.model`, then the selected
agent's native `model`, then `config.model`, then PathGrade's default. Resolve
these choices before credential staging. Other agents retain their models. All
profile models must use the main model's provider; mixed-provider profiles fail
explicitly until credential routing supports them.

Permission pattern order is preserved. Top-level overrides replace matching
default rules; `'*': 'deny'` also removes inherited tool allows. Native top-level
tool switches replace matching defaults, with explicit permission overrides taking
precedence. Native per-agent permissions remain native overrides. Headless `ask` rules fail before staging.
Permissions cannot exceed strict filesystem mounts. Strict MCP and Scenario V2
remain unsupported and explicitly rejected. See [strict isolation](opencode-strict-isolation.md).

Native custom tools can intentionally replace built-ins by name. Supply explicit
action mappings when their semantics differ. Mappings cannot claim MCP invocation
or approval. Native names, arguments, call IDs, results, statuses, and timings
remain visible. Batch file arrays produce one event with a bounded file summary.
Domain failures returned as text remain results, separate from provider execution
status; consumers interpret their own result contracts. No failure-text heuristic
is applied.

The ordinary CLI stream contains parent-session evidence only. A completed
`task` does not establish complete child tool calls, child usage, or domain
success. Mixed-session rejection stays in place; no complete child trace is
advertised.

Declare profile files in eval `comparisonInputs` and affected-selection
inputs so changes invalidate baselines. Deterministic configuration and scripted
contracts do not make live model-generated output deterministic.

Synthetic contracts cover ordinary and strict execution, native tool replacement,
explicit model override, primary/reviewer instructions and models, permission
denials, plugin rejection, domain results, custom subprocess isolation, and
continuation. Linux CI runs these checks in the existing strict job; macOS checks
run locally. Production consumer compatibility is a separate acceptance step.

# macOS trial process cleanup

The macOS feasibility probe found that killing a process group leaves detached children alive. `launchd` cleanup also left the detached child alive. PID/parent polling alone cannot recover ownership once a double-forked child is reparented.

`native/macos-process-supervisor.c` provides the tested replacement. It runs inside the same Seatbelt sandbox as the command. macOS checks process-info and signal permission against `target same-sandbox`, so the supervisor can find its detached and reparented children without treating other trials or host processes as its own. It stops all live sandbox members, repeats enumeration until every member is stopped, kills them, and verifies that none remain alive. It only then acknowledges cleanup over a private control pipe.

The native supervisor refuses an unsandboxed invocation and verifies that it can enumerate and signal its child before allowing that child to execute the command. A private startup pipe holds the child until preflight succeeds; EOF aborts startup without requiring signals. The trusted macOS profile must grant process-info and signals only to `target same-sandbox`, grant `kern.proc.all` for enumeration, and expose the supervisor and command as read-only executable inputs. Process metadata is not hidden by a Linux-style PID namespace.

The internal `spawnMacOSSupervised` adapter preserves the command's standard streams and exit status. Disposal closes the private lifetime pipe and awaits the cleanup acknowledgement; it must not kill the supervisor's process group. Children do not inherit the control pipe. If the host disconnects, the supervisor performs cleanup automatically. If the supervisor crashes, is killed, or does not acknowledge cleanup within the bounded timeout, disposal rejects. Its caller must retain the trial's private state and report that cleanup could not be verified, instead of treating it as a successful disposal.

Regression coverage includes double-forked detached children, concurrent trials and a live host process, natural completion, stdin/stdout and nonzero exit status, a lost control pipe, a suspended supervisor, a killed supervisor, and unsandboxed invocation. The updated standalone macOS validation passes all 33 checks on macOS 26.6.2 arm64 with Node 22.18.0 and OpenCode 1.18.14.

PathGrade's public strict mode uses this adapter for admitted agent processes and workspace commands on macOS. Cancellation, turn completion, and workspace disposal wait for verified cleanup; failed disposal retains private state and repeats the error on subsequent disposal attempts, including through the public agent API. Cancellation timeout rejects the same cleanup promise used by every waiter. Strict roots carry a retention marker from creation, so a later startup does not remove them based only on a dead host PID. The package includes the universal `native/bin/macos-process-supervisor` executable, its integrity manifest, and no installation hook. Regression tests execute the shipped binary directly.

Maintainers can rebuild the executable with `node scripts/build-macos-supervisor.mjs` on macOS with Apple's development toolchain. The script compiles both arm64 and x86_64 slices, combines them, applies an ad-hoc signature, and records binary/source hashes. Commit the binary and manifest together with source changes. This toolchain is a maintainer prerequisite only. macOS 11 is the compilation target, not a claim that every release has been validated; the integration proof currently covers macOS 26.6.2 arm64. Intel execution still needs validation on Intel hardware.

Workspace startup gives the OS preflight 15 seconds to finish. If preflight fails or times out, PathGrade disposes the execution boundary before removing private state. macOS disposal can take up to another 15 seconds. If cleanup cannot be verified, startup reports both failures and retains the private root, just as normal workspace disposal does.

# Experimental Codex-authenticated ChatGPT judge

Status: **experimental**. W0b passed for the direct
`@openai-oauth/core@2.0.0` Responses mapping, and W0c passed for acquiring a
managed ChatGPT access session from Codex App Server.

## Install and authenticate

Install Pathgrade and sign in once with Codex. Pathgrade installs its pinned
OAuth runtime dependency automatically:

```bash
yarn add -D @wix/pathgrade
codex login
```

Pathgrade starts a short-lived `codex app-server` child over stdio, calls only
the auth-status RPC, then closes it before making the direct judge request. It
does not read, copy, or write `~/.codex/auth.json`, receive a refresh token,
open a local port, or start a Codex model thread. After a real upstream 401 it
asks Codex to refresh, retries once, and otherwise fails closed.

## Inject explicitly

Codex agents select this judge automatically when neither `OPENAI_API_KEY` nor
`OPENAI_BASE_URL` is present. The judge uses the resolved Codex model (Luna by
default) with high reasoning effort. Passing `evaluate(agent, scorers, { llm })`
remains the highest-precedence override. Explicit construction is available for
other agents and custom flows:

```typescript
import { createChatGptOAuthJudgeLLM } from '@wix/pathgrade/openai-oauth';
import { evaluate, judge } from '@wix/pathgrade';

const llm = createChatGptOAuthJudgeLLM({
    model: 'gpt-5.6-sol',
    reasoningEffort: 'high',
    requestTimeoutMs: 60_000,
});

const result = await evaluate(agent, [
    judge('quality', { rubric: 'Apply the frozen rubric.', model: 'gpt-5.6-sol' }),
], { llm });
```

The scorer model must exactly equal the factory model. There is no auth-file,
API-key, base-URL, login callback, provider fallback, model rewrite, or default
provider registration. Plain calls expose zero tools. Tool judges expose only
their declared Pathgrade schemas through the existing bounded tool registry.

## Stable public failures

- `OAUTH_CONFIG_INVALID`
- `OAUTH_DEPENDENCY_UNAVAILABLE`
- `OAUTH_CODEX_UNAVAILABLE`
- `OAUTH_CODEX_LOGIN_REQUIRED`
- `OAUTH_AUTH_TIMEOUT`
- `OAUTH_MODEL_MISMATCH`
- `OAUTH_MODEL_UNAVAILABLE`
- `OAUTH_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`
- `OAUTH_UPSTREAM_RATE_LIMITED`
- `OAUTH_UPSTREAM_FAILED`
- `OAUTH_PROTOCOL_RESPONSE_INVALID`

Tokens, Codex paths, auth JSON, prompts, App Server stderr/RPC text, upstream
bodies, and tool results are never included in public errors. Failures never
fall back to another provider.

## Repository-only verification

These maintainer probes run from a source checkout and are not included in the
published npm package. Run them from the repository root.

The no-cost installed-binary probe reports only version, auth-mode booleans,
and its ADAPT/STOP verdict:

```bash
yarn smoke:codex-auth
```

The explicit paid live suite uses only the active Codex login. It exercises
direct plain and bounded `readFile` judges, then a real keyless Codex app-server
agent followed by automatically selected plain and `readFile` judges:

```bash
yarn test:evals:judge-oauth:live
```

It writes redacted reports to `.pathgrade/judge-oauth-live-smoke.{json,md}` and
`.pathgrade/codex-oauth-agent-judge-e2e.json`.
Any `@openai-oauth/core` or Codex protocol upgrade must rerun W0b, W0c, and
the live smoke.

# PathGrade strict filesystem isolation

`workspace` continues to copy the project directly into the trial working directory. No launch-subdirectory option was added. Keep evals, scorers, golden fixtures, and harness sources out of that input copy.

Ordinary OpenCode, Claude Agent SDK, and Codex app-server support an explicit macOS or Linux execution boundary. The OpenCode example is:

```ts
const agent = await createAgent({
    agent: 'opencode',
    opencodeExecutable: '/opt/opencode/opencode', // existing pinned executable contract
    workspace: stagedProjectRoot,
    skillDir: stagedCandidateSkill,
    isolation: {
        mode: 'strict',
        readOnlyPaths: [installedDependencyRoot, '/opt/node-runtime'],
    },
    env: { ANTHROPIC_API_KEY },
});
// Default copyIgnore excludes node_modules. Link the declared dependency tree after copying.
await fs.symlink(installedDependencyRoot, path.join(agent.workspace, 'node_modules'));
```

`StrictIsolationOptions` is exported from `@wix/pathgrade`. Omission preserves the existing directory-copy behavior. Strict mode has no fallback.

## Boundary and inputs

On Linux, PathGrade launches `/usr/bin/bwrap` with a fresh filesystem root, user/PID/IPC/UTS/cgroup namespaces, no capabilities, and nested user namespaces disabled. Only the trial's workspace, HOME, and TMP are writable host mounts. `/tmp` is separate scratch space. XDG directories and package-manager caches live in the private HOME. The host PATH is replaced with system binaries plus declared runtime locations.

Read-only system mounts are `/usr/bin`, `/usr/lib`, `/usr/lib64`, `/bin`, `/lib`, and `/lib64` when present, plus DNS/host resolution and TLS certificate files. The resolved OpenCode executable is mounted individually. The host root, HOME, checkout, sibling trials, and scorer sources are not mounted. Network access remains available for provider APIs and workspace tooling; this is a filesystem/process boundary, not network isolation. Do not run filesystem services reachable by the agent that expose excluded host files.

On macOS, PathGrade uses the built-in `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` with a deny-by-default Seatbelt profile. It allows reads of selected system runtime files, the OpenCode executable, and declared dependencies, and writes only within the trial workspace, HOME, and TMP. File content access to host scorers, checkouts, HOME, and sibling trials is denied. Directory metadata and process metadata are not hidden as they are by Linux namespaces. IP networking remains available; access to host Unix sockets is denied except the system DNS resolver.

The npm package includes an ad-hoc signed universal supervisor binary for Apple Silicon and Intel. There is no compiler prerequisite, install hook, additional download, or Bubblewrap dependency on macOS. The supervisor runs inside the sandbox and stops and reaps sandbox members, including detached descendants. Turns, cancellation, and disposal require its cleanup acknowledgement. A crashed, killed, or unresponsive supervisor causes an error and retention of private state; PathGrade never reports successful cleanup in that case. See [macOS cleanup](macos-process-cleanup.md).

`readOnlyPaths` contains absolute, canonical, trusted runtime/dependency files or self-contained trees, available at the same paths. Do not declare a checkout, host HOME, eval directory, broad temporary directory, or other sensitive source as a dependency. Declared roots cannot contain the harness working directory or overlap writable trial mounts. Each dependency tree is audited independently: workspace-package links escaping that tree and special files are rejected. Filter workspace links before declaring a monorepo dependency install. For package managers with external stores, stage a self-contained dependency tree first.

Staged workspace/HOME/TMP symlinks must resolve within the trial or a declared dependency. Symlinks created later cannot reveal an excluded target. On Linux, an attempted write to a hidden absolute path can create an isolated scratch-file shadow if its parent exists; it cannot mutate or reveal the corresponding host file.

Shared dependencies are read-only even when the launching user is root. For installs that modify dependencies, use a private workspace dependency tree instead of linking the read-only tree. Stage required credential files into private HOME, or authenticate using `agent.exec()` there; host credential symlinks are inaccessible. Existing OpenCode provider credential filtering still applies.

The same OS boundary wraps admitted agent processes and `agent.exec()`/setup commands. Plugins, custom tools, and subprocesses inherit the OS sandbox. Linux PID namespace teardown and the macOS supervisor clean up descendants; strict OpenCode cleanup removes and recreates HOME without following a replaced HOME root or XDG parent links, and workspace disposal joins active launcher processes before removing private state. Session replies reuse the same mounts and private OpenCode state.

## Platform and route admission

On Linux, requires Bubblewrap >= 0.8 at `/usr/bin/bwrap`, and permission to create all requested namespaces. The exact mount/namespace command is probed before an agent or setup command runs. Missing Bubblewrap, blocked user namespaces, incompatible flags, or other mount failures reject workspace creation and remove staged state. On macOS, the bundled supervisor and built-in sandbox are probed before execution; missing or incompatible components fail without a fallback. Windows rejects strict mode before staging. Apple deprecated `sandbox-exec`, so future macOS releases require validation before being advertised as supported.

Scenario V2/ACP and all current MCP declarations are rejected with strict isolation. Their host-authoritative tool hosts are separate execution paths and cannot be advertised as isolated by wrapping only the OpenCode process. Cursor and Codex exec also reject strict mode. Claude and Codex app-server currently require API-key authentication; host OAuth and Keychain links are not admitted for these routes. Ordinary generated MCP is rejected because it starts tools from harness-owned modules; do not declare the harness as a dependency to bypass this rejection.

The CI workflow runs strict isolation and native Codex checks in a separate Linux job, using Wix's existing `self-hosted` runner scale-set label. This scale set provides Linux x64 runners; it does not expose a separate `Linux` scheduling label. It uses a Node 22 Debian container with namespace-compatible security options, standard Docker devices and capabilities, and no privileged flag. These options permit Bubblewrap to create namespaces and mount fresh `/proc` inside the container. The job copies the workspace into the container filesystem under `/tmp/agent-evals`, reuses the repository's immutable Yarn installation, and installs Bubblewrap through apt. It receives no evaluation secrets; copied build files disappear with the container. PathGrade still enforces its explicit mounts, dropped capabilities, and disabled nested user namespaces around every strict trial. The ordinary Agent Evals job runs separately without a container. macOS checks run locally, outside CI; no macOS CI runner is available. Missing Linux sandbox capability fails CI without fallback.

## Deterministic verification and handoff

On 2026-10-09, the Linux suite passed as UID 1000 in a Linux ARM64 Node 22 test container with Bubblewrap 0.8.0 and permitted namespaces. The container was privileged to enable namespace creation; the evaluated processes themselves were unprivileged and capability-free. A second run in a container with its default restricted security policy rejected creation during the namespace probe with no fallback.

macOS verification on 2026-10-09 used macOS 26.6.2 arm64, Node 22.18.0, and OpenCode 1.18.14. SDK tests cover concurrent trials, native/custom/shell/child access, escape symlinks, immutable dependencies, TypeScript checking, session continuation, cancellation and detached-child disposal, failed cleanup retaining state, and hostile XDG-parent links. Native tests use the bundled executable and verify its source/integrity manifest. A real OpenCode session against a scripted local HTTPS provider verifies a bash tool, workspace writes, denied scorer reads, and session continuation without paid model calls. The actual npm tarball also passed the real OpenCode check with install scripts disabled. The build, repository quality checks, and 316 targeted tests passed (four skips for platform or existing gated coverage). The universal Intel slice is compiled but has not been exercised on Intel hardware. Linux and macOS runtime policies should be validated independently on deployment machines.

For steps 2–3, copy the declared production configuration/tool bundle into managed private HOME/XDG state before first turn, then reuse this boundary. Its runtime dependencies must be declared read-only inputs or private copies. Keep the ordinary spawn path's boundary intact. Support separate agent-facing tool hosts inside the same boundary or continue rejecting their routes explicitly. The consumer migration must replace dependency/auth links into host workspace packages with audited dependency trees and private credentials. Production agent selection, native configuration/tool loading, action mappings, trace semantics, and consumer migration remain subsequent work.

## Shared harness integration

Runtime requirements live in `src/agents/runtime-requirements.ts`: executable resolution, admitted authentication, trusted configuration files, and private directory variables are declared separately from protocol handling. Workspace preparation owns staging and boundary creation. Strict roots are marked for retention at creation: host death alone cannot prove descendant cleanup, so automatic stale cleanup never removes abandoned strict roots. Successful verified disposal removes them; unverified or crashed roots require explicit cleanup after their processes have been stopped. agent-evals reuses the public PathGrade API without adding another isolation layer.

Claude uses the existing SDK spawn hook. The SDK's direct kill calls are translated into boundary cancellation; exit is published only after verified cleanup. Auto-memory settings are staged outside writable trial directories as a read-only input, so the SDK does not create an inaccessible host-temp settings file. `CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR` points to private trial TMP.

Codex app-server uses the existing RPC transport with the shared boundary for the conversation lifetime. `CODEX_HOME` is private. Native binaries and official npm launchers are resolved to the native executable before launch. The system requirements policy file is an explicit read-only runtime input, including an absent-file rule on macOS so the CLI can distinguish absence from denied access. Codex's inner sandbox uses `danger-full-access` only when PathGrade provides the outer OS boundary, avoiding incompatible nested sandbox creation. PathGrade's filesystem and process restrictions remain enforced around the complete process.

Harness contract tests exercise the Claude spawn hook and Codex RPC transport on macOS and Linux. The RPC fixture uses Node to speak the protocol; it does not establish native Codex Linux compatibility. Actual Claude SDK turns against a local scripted HTTPS provider pass on macOS arm64 and Linux arm64, including Bash execution, denied scorer reads, workspace writes, and continuation. No paid model calls are needed. The actual npm tarball, packed with install scripts disabled, passed real OpenCode, Claude, and Codex app-server sessions on macOS arm64. Each check verifies a tool turn, denied scorer reads, workspace writes, and chat continuation against a local scripted provider. Native Codex 0.149.0-alpha.4, resolved through its official npm launcher, also passed on Linux arm64 as UID 1000 with Bubblewrap 0.8.0: private API-key login, thread startup, tool execution, scorer-read denial, workspace writes, and continuation. The Linux regression run passed 126 tests with 10 platform-specific skips. The dedicated Linux CI job runs the native Codex check as well as the protocol fixture.
